keyQuestions.text: Which git operation families can be classified reliably from the Bash command before execution?
Which repository, worktree, index, remote, config, and account state is genuinely available before each candidate command runs?
Which high-cost failures beyond the five observed incidents warrant new advisory rules?
How often would each candidate fire in real repository history, and what is the defensible noise threshold?
Which dangerous-looking operations should remain silent because enforcement already owns them or preflight state is unavailable or too noisy?

carriedForwardOpenQuestions: Which bounded state probes make destructive-history predicates precise enough?
How often do state-gated candidates match without exact argv telemetry?
Which staging and commit predicates detect cross-session contamination without warning on intentional multi-path commits?
Which positive local coordination and remote/account facts justify advisories despite unavoidable race windows?
What final candidate tiers, coalescing rules, latency limits, and aggregate alert budget keep advisories below the attention threshold?
No key questions remain; implementation must validate the retained classifier in privacy-preserving shadow mode.

keyFindings.text: The evaluator accepts only command text today; direct branch creation and --no-verify are command-only, while most valuable destructive candidates need bounded repository-state probes.
Broad reflog prevalence was amend 0.47%, rebase 2.97%, reset 13.56%, and commit 73.55%; broad family warnings above roughly 1% require state gating.

Retained destructive rules can be narrowed to positive state: published containment, nonempty exact-path overwrite, clean dry-run removals, unique branch commits, dirty or active forced worktree removal, unrescued stash entries, and nonempty immediate-expiry/prune exposure.

Routine and recovery forms should stay silent where Git already blocks or preserves state, including branch -d, checked-out branch deletion, ordinary dirty worktree removal, clean without force, and conflicted stash pop.

Retain staging advisories only when exact broad/selective commands expose objective mismatches: held-back staged paths, one-sided inferred renames, forced ignored files, or reproducible expansion beyond explicit paths.
Git state has no session-owner field and PreToolUse sees only the pre-hook candidate, so advisories must be neutral and cannot guarantee final commit contents.

Detached or linked pushes to a branch checked out elsewhere and manual wrapper publication have predictable local coordination consequences, but push success and follower reconciliation remain unknown.
Current pre-push enforcement skips tags and does not own force/delete/mirror/prune or destructive multi-ref semantics; these require positive destination evidence and coalesced advisories.
Twenty-three exact command/state rules survive ranking; fourteen broad, unavailable, enforcement-owned, or over-budget classes are rejected.
Shadow-mode targets are under 0.5 alerts per 100 eligible invocations per rule and under 2 per 100 aggregate, with hard ceilings of 1 and 3; emit one coalesced line at most.

ruledOutDirections: Unconditional warnings for generic commit, reset, rebase, pull, or push
Duplicating existing pre-push branch naming and permission enforcement
Using Git history as exact argv telemetry
Treating raceable remote snapshots or post-execution outcomes as facts
Using absent remote containment as proof that history is unpublished
Path-count-only, cross-top-level, and unconditional selective-commit warnings
Predicting interactive or stdin path selections and hook-time final commit state
Generic push, account, detached-worktree, and nondestructive multi-ref warnings
Duplicating pre-push naming and permission blockers
Treating gh identity, API permission, or network snapshots as remote outcome proof
Network probes, full object scans, and all-worktree sweeps in the synchronous path
Generic filter-rewrite name matching without a validated mutating predicate
